analysis.investment_thesis: Marc Technocrats is a debt-free micro-cap consulting firm posting strong ROCE (36%) and 41% net profit CAGR — but at INR 48 Cr revenue, it lacks scale, institutional validation, and critically, its earnings are not converting to cash. The consulting model offers no durable moat, and the FCF/Net Income ratio of ~43% in FY2025 fails my quality threshold by nearly half.
key_strengths: Debt-free balance sheet with ROCE of 36.27% — capital efficiency is genuinely impressive for its size
Revenue and profit scaling together: 35% revenue CAGR with 41% net profit CAGR signals operating leverage
100% OCF positivity over 4 years with zero finance cost — no leverage risk
key_risks: Earnings quality is alarming: FY2025 net profit jumped to 7 Cr but OCF stayed flat at 5 Cr and FCF at 3 Cr — FCF/NI is ~43%, well below my 80% floor
Consulting has no moat — revenue depends on relationships and key people, not a durable structural advantage
73.55% promoter holding with FII at 0.27% and DII at 1.38% — virtually no institutional scrutiny or liquidity
red_flags: FCF/Net Income of ~43% in FY2025 — earnings growing but cash is not; working capital or receivables likely building
Exchange listing shows 'YHD-ERR' — data integrity concern, possibly SME platform with very thin float
At INR 48 Cr revenue, the entire business could hinge on 2-3 client relationships — concentration risk is unknowable
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Invert first: what makes this a bad investment? A consulting firm at INR 48 Cr revenue has no pricing power, no recurring revenue lock-in, and no asset base that compounds. The ROCE looks stellar at 36%, but in people-businesses this often reflects under-investment rather than genuine competitive advantage — the moment key personnel leave, the moat evaporates. More damning is the FY2025 cash conversion collapse: net profit doubled from 3 Cr to 7 Cr, yet free cash flow stayed anchored at 3 Cr. That divergence is not a rounding error — it's a structural signal that earnings quality is deteriorating even as headline numbers improve.

The shareholding pattern compounds my concern. With promoters at 73.55% and institutions at a combined 1.65%, there is no independent governance scrutiny. Micro-cap consulting firms with high promoter control and poor FCF conversion are precisely the category where accounting creativity tends to flourish. The company may be perfectly honest — but I cannot verify that, and Munger's rule is simple: if you can't understand it deeply, you don't own it. The exchange listing anomaly is an additional data-integrity flag I cannot dismiss. Pass.
